description: Windows Security events related to account sign-in, sign-in failures, authentication protocols, session endings, and account lockouts.

source.note: Event availability depends on Windows version, audit policy, role, and configuration.

4610.headline: An authentication component was loaded
4610.plain_english: Windows loaded a component that handles logins. This is normal at startup. If an unfamiliar component loads after a change, investigate.
4610.technical_description: Security event 4610: authentication package was loaded by the Local Security Authority.

who.SubjectUserName: Account associated with the event, if recorded

4610.when: Time Windows recorded the package load.
4610.why_it_matters: Unfamiliar authentication packages can be a sign of tampering with the login pipeline.
normal_when: Standard security package present in baseline
suspicious_when: A package not present in baseline loads
Package loads after an unexplained system change
what_to_do: Verify the package is expected on this machine
Compare to a known-good baseline

severity.high: Unfamiliar package correlated with other suspicious changes

4610.important_note: Package load alone does not prove malicious activity.

4611.headline: A sign-in component registered with Windows
4611.plain_english: A login-process component registered with Windows. Normal for known Windows components; unfamiliar names are worth review.
4611.technical_description: Security event 4611: a trusted logon process registered with the Local Security Authority.

where.LogonProcessName: Name of the registered logon process

4611.why_it_matters: Unexpected logon processes can indicate tampering with authentication.
what_to_do: Verify the process name is expected

severity.high: Unfamiliar process plus other suspicious activity

4611.important_note: Registration alone is not evidence of compromise.

4622.headline: A Windows security package was loaded
4622.plain_english: Windows loaded a security package used for authentication. Normal for known packages.
4622.technical_description: Security event 4622: a security package was loaded by the Local Security Authority.

where.PackageName: Name of the loaded security package

4622.when: Time Windows recorded the package load.
4622.why_it_matters: Unfamiliar security packages can indicate tampering.
what_to_do: Verify the package name against baseline

severity.high: Unfamiliar package plus other suspicious changes

4622.important_note: Package load alone does not prove malicious activity.

4624.headline: A sign-in succeeded
4624.plain_english: Someone successfully signed in. The fields tell you who, from where, and how (local keyboard, Remote Desktop, network share, service). A successful sign-in is normal — what matters is whether it was expected.
4624.technical_description: Security event 4624: successful logon. LogonType indicates method: 2=interactive, 3=network, 5=service, 7=unlock, 8=network-cleartext, 9=runas, 10=RemoteInteractive, 11=cached.
4624.when: Time Windows recorded the successful logon.
4624.why_it_matters: Successful sign-ins establish who accessed a device, from where, and how.
normal_when: User logging into their own PC with LogonType 2
IT support RDP with LogonType 10 and a ticket
Service account starting a service with LogonType 5
suspicious_when: Logon for a non-24/7 user at 3am
LogonType 3 (network) by a user who normally doesn't use network logons
Logon from a workstation you don't recognize
what_to_do: Confirm the user signed in as expected
Check the source IP against expected networks
If unrecognized: disable the account and start incident response

severity.low: Account, device, time, and logon type all match expectation

4624.important_note: A successful logon is not automatically suspicious — LogonType and source matter more than the event alone.

4625.headline: A sign-in attempt failed
4625.plain_english: Someone tried to sign in but Windows rejected it — usually a wrong password. One failure is common (typo, saved password on another device). Many failures in a row may mean someone is guessing passwords.
4625.technical_description: Security event 4625: failed logon. FailureReason and SubStatus indicate why (e.g. bad password, account disabled, account expired).
4625.when: Time Windows recorded the failed sign-in.
4625.why_it_matters: Repeated failures against the same account or from unfamiliar sources often indicate password guessing or an outdated saved credential.
normal_when: An old saved credential fails on a scheduled task
suspicious_when: Many failures against one account in a short time
Failures distributed across many accounts (password spraying)
what_to_do: Check whether the source IP is expected
Review repeated failures for the same account
Escalate if the pattern suggests password guessing

severity.high: Repeated failures plus other suspicious events, or spraying pattern

4625.important_note: A failed sign-in does not automatically mean hacking.

4634.headline: A sign-in session ended
4634.plain_english: A logon session ended. Sessions correspond to successful logons; matching the Logon ID with a 4624 shows how long the session lasted.
4634.technical_description: Security event 4634: logon session terminated. Use TargetLogonId to correlate with the originating 4624.

where.Computer: Machine that recorded the session end

4634.why_it_matters: Helps bracket the activity that happened during a session.
suspicious_when: Session ends within seconds of a suspicious logon
what_to_do: Correlate the Logon ID with the matching 4624
4634.important_note: Session end does not necessarily mean the user clicked Sign out.

4647.headline: A user started signing out
4647.plain_english: The user clicked sign out (as opposed to the machine shutting down or the session ending for another reason).

where.Computer: Machine that recorded the logoff request

4647.when: Time Windows recorded the logoff request.
4647.why_it_matters: Distinguishes user-initiated logoff from other session terminations.
suspicious_when: Sign out unexpected for the user
Sign out immediately after suspicious activity
what_to_do: Confirm with the user that the sign-out was intentional

severity.high: Part of correlated suspicious session activity

4647.important_note: Indicates the logoff was initiated, not why.

4648.headline: A program signed in using specified credentials
4648.plain_english: A program logged in using a different account than the current user — for example, 'Run as different user' or a scheduled task running as a service account.
4648.technical_description: Security event 4648: logon attempted with explicitly supplied credentials. Used by Runas, PsExec, and scheduled tasks.

who.SubjectUserName: Account whose session initiated the action

4648.when: Time Windows recorded the explicit-credentials logon.
4648.why_it_matters: Normal for admin tools and service accounts; suspicious if the user, account, or target is unexpected.
normal_when: Admin using Runas to perform support
Scheduled task running as a service account
Accessing a remote resource with alternate credentials
suspicious_when: Unexpected account is used for explicit logon
Process is not one that normally uses explicit creds (e.g. cmd.exe or powershell.exe suddenly appearing)
what_to_do: Confirm the initiating user expected the action
Verify the process and target resource
Confirm the supplied account is authorized for the task

severity.high: Correlated with credential misuse or unauthorized access

4648.important_note: Explicit credential use is not automatically malicious.

4649.headline: A possible authentication replay was detected
4649.plain_english: Windows detected what looks like a replay attack — authentication information was reused in a way that suggests interception. Take this seriously if corroborated.
4649.technical_description: Security event 4649: replay attack detected during authentication.
4649.why_it_matters: Replay detection is security-relevant and should be investigated with the original event and surrounding authentication activity.
what_to_do: Review the complete event details and source device
Correlate with nearby authentication and network events
Follow IR process if validated
4649.important_note: Preserve the original event; investigate before concluding an attack succeeded.

4740.headline: A user account was locked
4740.plain_english: A user account was locked because of too many wrong password attempts. Often caused by a forgotten password or an outdated saved password on another device. Repeated lockouts can indicate password guessing.
4740.technical_description: Security event 4740: account lockout triggered by reaching the domain/computer lockout threshold.

where.CallerComputerName: Machine that reported the lockout request, if recorded

4740.why_it_matters: Repeated lockouts can be the first sign of an active password-guessing attack.
normal_when: Stale saved credential on another device retrying
suspicious_when: Repeated lockouts for the same account
Many different accounts locked at once
Lockouts originating from a machine the user doesn't use
what_to_do: Confirm the user was trying to sign in
Check the caller computer
Correlate with failures (4625, 4771)

severity.high: Multiple accounts locked, or lockouts correlated with failures

4740.important_note: Lockout alone doesn't prove an attacker caused it.

4768.headline: A Kerberos sign-in ticket was requested
4768.plain_english: A user asked the domain controller for a Kerberos sign-in ticket. This is the first step of a domain login and normal for domain users. Unusual failure patterns or unusual sources are worth review.
4768.technical_description: Security event 4768: Kerberos TGT (Ticket-Granting Ticket) request on a domain controller. Status indicates success or failure reason.

who.TargetUserName: Account the ticket was requested for

where.Computer: Domain controller that recorded the request

4768.when: Time the domain controller recorded the request.
4768.why_it_matters: Unexpected request patterns can indicate domain authentication problems or suspicious activity.
normal_when: Normal user sign-in on a domain-joined machine
suspicious_when: Requests for service accounts from unusual sources
Spike in requests for one account
what_to_do: Check the account and client address
Review the result and failure code
Correlate unusual requests with 4769 and 4771
4768.important_note: A ticket request is a normal part of Kerberos authentication.

4769.headline: Access to a domain service was requested
4769.plain_english: A user asked for a ticket to access a specific domain service (file share, database, etc.). Shows which accounts access which services.
4769.technical_description: Security event 4769: Kerberos service ticket request.

where.Computer: Domain controller that recorded the request

4769.when: Time the domain controller recorded the request.
4769.why_it_matters: Service-ticket activity shows which accounts access what — useful for spotting lateral movement.
suspicious_when: Account requests a service it shouldn't access
Service ticket for a service account from a workstation that shouldn't have one
what_to_do: Confirm the account should access the requested service
Review unusual service names and client addresses
Correlate with 4624 and 4768

severity.high: Correlated with other evidence of compromise

4769.important_note: Service-ticket request is normal domain activity.

4770.headline: A Kerberos service ticket was renewed
4770.plain_english: A Kerberos ticket was renewed to extend a session. Routine in most environments.
4770.technical_description: Security event 4770: Kerberos service ticket renewed.

where.Computer: Domain controller that recorded the renewal

4770.when: Time the domain controller recorded the renewal.
4770.why_it_matters: Usually routine; unusual patterns are worth a look.
suspicious_when: Renewal from a client that shouldn't access the service
what_to_do: Confirm the account and service are expected
4770.important_note: Ticket renewal is normal Kerberos operation.

4771.headline: A Kerberos sign-in check failed
4771.plain_english: A Kerberos login attempt failed the pre-authentication check — usually a wrong password. Repeated failures can indicate password guessing.
4771.technical_description: Security event 4771: Kerberos pre-authentication failed. FailureCode indicates reason (0x18 = bad password).

where.Computer: Domain controller that recorded the failure

4771.when: Time the domain controller recorded the failure.
4771.why_it_matters: Repeated failures from unfamiliar sources suggest incorrect credentials, misconfiguration, or password guessing.
normal_when: Isolated failure with known cause (wrong password)
what_to_do: Review the failure code and account
Check whether the source device is recognized
Correlate with 4625 and 4768

severity.high: Failures plus other suspicious authentication evidence

4771.important_note: A pre-authentication failure does not by itself prove password spraying.

4772.headline: A Kerberos ticket request failed
4772.plain_english: A Kerberos ticket request failed. The event's result code tells you why — read it before drawing conclusions.
4772.technical_description: Security event 4772: Kerberos TGT request failed.

where.Computer: Domain controller that recorded the failure

4772.when: Time Windows recorded the failed request.
4772.why_it_matters: Repeated unexplained failures may indicate credential or configuration problems.
what_to_do: Inspect the complete event and failure info
Check the account and source device
Correlate with other Kerberos events
4772.important_note: Confirm the event meaning and available fields before parsing.

4774.headline: An account was mapped for sign-in
4774.plain_english: An account was mapped to a logon — used in authentication flows that map an external identity to a Windows account.
4774.technical_description: Security event 4774: account mapped for logon (identity mapping in some authentication scenarios).
4774.why_it_matters: Unexpected mappings may indicate misuse in environments that map external accounts.
normal_when: Configured mapping in a mapped-account environment
suspicious_when: Mapping that leads to a privileged account
what_to_do: Verify the account and mapping configuration

severity.high: Unapproved mapping linked to suspicious access

4774.important_note: Mapping alone does not prove unauthorized access.

4775.headline: Windows could not map an account for sign-in
4775.plain_english: An authentication mapping attempt failed. Usually a configuration or account problem; recurring unexplained failures deserve review.
4775.technical_description: Security event 4775: account could not be mapped for logon.
4775.why_it_matters: May indicate misconfiguration or suspicious activity.
what_to_do: Check the account and mapping configuration
Correlate with 4625
4775.important_note: A mapping failure is not proof of an attack.

4776.headline: Windows checked NTLM sign-in credentials
4776.plain_english: Windows checked a username and password using NTLM, a legacy authentication protocol. Succeeds silently for older apps. Failures are usually more interesting than successes.
4776.technical_description: Security event 4776: NTLM credential validation on the authority (workstation or DC).
4776.why_it_matters: NTLM use may be expected in some environments; unexpected use or repeated failures can indicate legacy auth or suspicious activity.
normal_when: Expected legacy auth for a known app
what_to_do: Confirm NTLM is expected for this account/device
Review the validation result and source workstation
Correlate failures with 4625 and 4771

severity.medium: Unexpected NTLM use or repeated failures

4776.important_note: Records credential validation, not the final resource accessed.

4777.headline: NTLM sign-in credentials could not be validated
4777.plain_english: NTLM credential validation failed — usually a wrong password, outdated cached credentials, or a password-guessing attempt.
4777.technical_description: Security event 4777: NTLM credential validation failed.
4777.why_it_matters: Repeated failures or unexpected NTLM use may indicate stale credentials, config issues, or an attack.
what_to_do: Check the account and source workstation
Review NTLM configuration and failure details
Correlate with 4625 and 4776
4777.important_note: A failed NTLM validation is not proof of an attack.

implementation_notes.verified_field: Only display a plain-English explanation when `verified` is true.
